newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council welcomes forthcoming W. Sahara talks.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council welcomes forthcoming W. Sahara talks.

text.p: Security Council members expressed satisfaction on Thursday that the parties to the dispute over Western Sahara had agreed to hold direct talks in Lisbon on June 23, under the auspices of envoy James Baker, the former U.S. Secretary of State.
Council president Sergei Lavrov of Russia said members "expect that these talks will lead to significant progress."

"The Security Council will closely follow developments on this issue and members of the council expect to continue to be regularly and fully informed about the progress made at these talks," Lavrov added.
The council had earlier been briefed on Western Sahara by the Under-Secretary-General for political affairs, Sir Kieran Prendergast.

The United Nations has been trying for years to organise a referendum to decide whether Western Sahara should be incorporated into Morocco, which controls most of the former Spanish colony, or become independent, as sought by the Algerian-backed Polisario Front.
The ballot, originally set for January 1992, has been repeatedly postponed because of a disagreement between the two sides over who should be eligible to vote.
Representatives of Morocco and Polisario were reported to have held unpublicised meetings last August and September in Geneva and Tangier, their first direct encounter since 1993.

During separate meetings in London earlier this month, Baker invited representatives of both sides, as well as of the neighbouring countries of Algeria and Mauritania, to a meeting in Lisbon next Monday.

Baker, who is Secretary-General Kofi Annan's personal envoy for Western Sahara, made an exploratory visit to North Africa in April. He has been asked to recommend whether the U.N. peace plan calling for a referendum can be carried out, or whether agreed adjustments can be made or other means found for resolving the dispute.
The Security Council last month renewed, until September 30, a 230-member U.N. observer force in the territory called the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO).
